properties.label: Over-the-Rhine - Cincinnati, Ohio, United States
properties.Description: Over-The-Rhine is a historical working-class neighborhood directly north of downtown Cincinnati. While I don't know as much about it as I do The Hill District, I currently know that It's been heavily gentrified, pushing out the original community and now serving the more wealthy. It still retains much of its older architecture though.

properties.label: Hill District - Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, United States
properties.Description: A once robust & lively black neighborhood that was mostly demolished during the era of urban renewal. It's famous for being one of the biggest stops for jazz music, with musicians driving between Chicago and New York stopping to play at clubs & venues. It was incredibly vital for black culture in Pittsburgh and had an incredibly tight knit community. Once urban renewal came along though, and cities sought to bring back a tax base through white families who fled to the suburbs, they decided to demolish the lower hill near downtown to build the Civic Arena, displacing thousands of residents in the name of "clearing blight." Over time this displaced the community of the Hill. Today, the Hill is making a slow comeback, but the harm the community & families of black Pittsburgh sustained in the process should not be forgotten.

properties.label: I-75 Corridor in Cincinnati
properties.Description: This corridor was built during urban renewal, and purposefully cut through predominantly black communities. The major interchange in the south connecting the Mill Creek Expressway, I-71, and I-75 (if I remember correctly) was also purposefully built to displace as many black and minority families as possible. The convenience of infrastructure can be at the cost of people.

properties.label: Brent Spencer Bridge
properties.Description: A very important double-decker truss bridge for Kentucky & Ohio, supporting I-71 traffic both ways. The top deck is for Kentucky-bound traffic, while the bottom is for Ohio-bound. Both the top and bottom deck feature 4 compact lanes with no shoulder, making it very dangerous. I believe that currently there is federal funding for supporting a new bridge, as well as funding to change the footprint of the massive interchange north of it.

properties.label: Quincy Street Floodwall
properties.Description: The extent of the wall itself is much longer than this, going towards downtown through Franklin Street, but this is the most striking part of it: it cuts straight down the center of the street and goes towards Bear Creek, where a small dam also is. It was first built after the Great Flood of 1937 which destroyed most of the Butchertown neighborhood that it's located in. The reason that this wall was built in the middle of the street rather than on one side or the other, is because the Army Corps of engineers wanted to avoid having to destroy the historical housing that was still standing.

properties.label: North 10th St./Rowan St. Floodwall
properties.Description: I don't know a lot about this one, I have to do more research. I'm pretty sure all the walls were connected at some point.
